title: Timberwolf encounter; childhood walk
description: Clara Grove describes walking home as a child through falling snow and spotting a timberwolf in the pastures. She explains how she walked slowly home, observing the animal's ears and behavior, before it moved through the cattle.

title: Railroad roundhouse; father's work
description: The conversation turns to Clara's father, who worked in a railroad roundhouse turning engines manually and cleaning fireboxes. She also shares anecdotes about firemen, engineers, and the prized nature of railroad jobs.

title: Redfield trains; early settlement
description: Clara describes the town of Redfield, South Dakota, as a busy railroad hub with multiple daily passenger trains and depots. She mentions nearby settlements and the significance of train travel in the community.

title: State capital fight; Charlie Blank
description: She details the political rivalry among Redfield, Aberdeen, and Huron for the South Dakota capital, including a story about a stolen building and the election of the charming Senator Charlie Blank.

title: Legislature antics; penny ante
description: Clara shares humorous stories about the early legislature being marooned by a snowstorm, holding mock sessions, and learning to play penny ante poker.

title: WCTU history; Frances Willard
description: The interviewer asks about the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, and Clara explains its international history, founder Frances Willard's vision, and the organization's broader goals beyond fighting liquor.

title: Temperance work; anti-liquor speeches
description: Clara discusses her personal involvement in the WCTU as a district president and state organizer, recounting specific experiences speaking to schoolchildren and confronting drinkers.

title: WCTU membership; white ribbon badge
description: She explains the WCTU membership dues and the significance of the white ribbon badge, also showing off a cane she made from a lilac tree limb.

title: Nursing homes; convalescent care
description: The discussion shifts to attitudes toward nursing homes, with Clara expressing her strong desire to remain independent and recounting a story about helping a friend enter a home.

title: Old-time remedies; childhood diseases
description: Clara introduces the topic of old-time remedies and discusses common ailments from her childhood such as fainting, ague, quinsy, and boils, and how they were treated.

title: Homemade coat; sewing project
description: She describes making a winter coat from a blanket using a magazine pattern and later selling the pattern to the publication.

title: More remedies; quinine for ague
description: Clara continues discussing old-time remedies, focusing on the use of quinine for ague and other historical medical practices.

title: Home remedies; herbal medicines
description: Clara Grove and the group discuss old-fashioned home remedies, beginning with treating skin conditions with salt water. She lists many herbal treatments including sage, hops, peppermint tea, sassafras, wild cherry bark, licorice, iodine, Lydia Pinkham's tonic, Smith Brothers cough drops, rhubarb, catnip, and witch hazel. She also tells of a missionary's wife gravely ill who was cured by an Indian doctor's herbs after American doctors failed her.

title: Poultices and cures; doctors making house calls
description: Grove recounts more remedies, including an onion poultice for pneumonia, turpentine, mustard plasters, hot black coffee, heated salt bags, warmed flatirons as heating pads, ginger tea, and the old practice of doctors bleeding patients with a small measuring cup. She recalls that doctors once made house calls for a dollar or two, never asking about Social Security, and that old-timers thought nothing of being a hundred miles from medical help. She inserts a memory of Mrs. Potts's improved flatiron design from around 1875.

title: Cosmetics; girls' hairstyles; Bernice Cunningham's story
description: Asked about old-time cosmetics, Grove remembers soap and water, rouge, face powder, lamp-heated curling irons, and rag curls, and she describes the long heavy braids worn by girls in Kirksville, Missouri, in the late 1890s. This leads to the story of Bernice Cunningham, a Moscow missionary who spent three years as a Japanese prisoner in the Philippines, lost her beautiful hair from hardship, and later cared for her father and dying brother, then renovated a rundown Tucson property.

title: Missionary Bells; Indian prince visitor; facing down animals
description: Grove mentions the Bells, missionaries to India, and an Indian prince who studied at the University of Idaho about forty years earlier and lectured in Troy about India and tiger hunting, claiming that looking a tiger in the eye prevents attack. She supports this with her own story of backing away from a neighbor's savage dog while holding its gaze, and a tale of a girl who stood laughing at a charging bull that never attacked her.

title: Travel mishaps; car troubles
description: Grove tells of misadventures while working and traveling up north, including wandering into rough country where she spotted what she took for a bear and escaped by walking a wire fence. She then recalls encounters with lumberjacks, a false holdup scare, a car fire near a Potlatch service station that a bystander doused with a bottled solution, and her opinion that there is no such thing as a rough lumberjack.

title: Project thanks and gifts
description: The interviewers present Grove with gifts, including stationery and a houseplant, and Isabel Miller reads a formal letter of thanks from the Women in Idaho's Heritage project. The letter describes the project's grant funding, its aim to preserve women's life experiences, and the archiving of Grove's taped interviews at the University of Idaho Library, and Grove expresses her own sense of urgency about contributing.

title: New Deal programs; relief and lost independence
description: Asked about the best era in her memory, Grove discusses Depression-era public works jobs such as mattress-making, rug-making, and the CCC boys' camp on the Pullman highway, including an incident with boys who stole a tractor. She then offers her opinion that Franklin Roosevelt's relief programs broke the spirit of independence in Americans, contrasting people who worked the system with her own ethic of hard work well into her seventies.

title: Relief and welfare; care of parents; return to God
description: Clara Grove criticizes abuses of relief and food stamps, contrasts past and present care for parents, and describes urgent religious calls for the nation to return to God.
